feedback: If 3/4 is placed too far from 0, count the equal jumps from 0: 'how many jumps of the same size?' — three quarter-jumps, landing before 1.

If fourths are drawn with 4 interior marks, shade each piece and count LENGTHS, not marks: four interior marks make five parts (fifths if equally spaced), but four equal parts need only 3 cuts inside.
If a point is read off by one (e.g. calling it 4/5), re-count the equal intervals from 0 rather than the ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.
learnerActions: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
activities.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks

feedback: If the point is read as 4/5, re-count the equal intervals from 0 — the marks are not the count; the lengths are.
If 3/4 is placed beyond 1, ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more than 1?' and place it inside 0–1.
If a child can read on a marked line but struggles on a blank one, rebuild the partition step by step before placing.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a given point (interpret) and placing a given fraction on a blank line (produce) are both needed; a fraction is the same size / the same point however it is represented.
learnerActions: On a 0–1 line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0, say what fraction the dot shows and explain how you know (four 1/6-lengths from 0 = 4/6).
On the same line, find and mark 1/2 (the 3rd mark, i.e. 3/6) and explain why it sits halfway.
Then take a blank 0–1 line and place 3/4 yourself: partition into 4 equal parts, count 3 parts from 0, land three-quarters of the way to 1.
Talk through each step aloud as you place it.
Also try ordering several fractions along one line to compare their positions.
activities.title: Read the point, then place the fraction

feedback: If 3/4 lands at three-quarters of the entire drawing, find and mark 1 first, then measure the quarter-length against the 0–1 segment only.
If a child says 3/4 would move when the line reaches 2, point back to the fixed 0–1 unit — the quarter-length is unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit is the 0–1 segment, not the whole drawn picture; with 0 and 1 kept in place, a/b keeps its position no matter how far the line is drawn. Lines extending past 1 let children show, and teachers address, errors such as placing 3/4 at or beyond 1, or 'between 3 and 4'.
learnerActions: On a line that extends past 1 (to 2 or beyond), first find and mark where 1 is.
Place 3/4 and check it sits below 1, NOT at three-quarters of the whole drawn line.
Answer: if this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Explain why not.
State that everything is measured against the fixed 0–1 length, whatever the drawing shows.
activities.title: Which segment is the unit?

feedback: If the child treats the area-model and line versions as different fractions, lay a fraction strip whose whole matches the 0–1 length against the line so the shaded length and the marked point coincide.
Prompt: 'Is 3/4 a different amount on the line than in the rectangle? Why or why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction has one magnitude whether shown as a shaded region or as a point/length on a line; connecting the two representations reinforces that a fraction is a single number.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a rectangle using the area model, then place 3/4 on a number line.
Explain how both show the same fraction — 'the same size, the same point'.
Measure a fraction strip against the line, using strips whose whole is the same length as the line's 0–1 segment, so the length and the position match (e.g. the 1/6 strip against sixths on the line).
activities.title: Compare with the area model
